entries.09c6f97836910b1b10dcdfb4995e2b3fa5d42cf9: <div sID="gen18464" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Ezek.5" sID="Ezek.5"/> <div eID="gen18464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18465" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18466" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have a further, and no less terrible, denunciation of the judgments of God, which were coming with all speed and force upon the Jewish nation, which would utterly ruin it; for when God judges he will overcome. This destruction of Judah and Jerusalem is here, I. Represented by a sign, the cutting, and burning, and scattering of hair, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.1-Ezek.5.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. That sign is expounded, and applied to Jerusalem. 1. Sin is charged upon Jerusalem as the cause of this desolation—contempt of God's law (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5-Ezek.5.7">ver. 5-7</reference>) and profanation of his sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">ver. 11</reference>. 2. Wrath is threatened, great wrath (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.8-Ezek.5.10">ver. 8-10</reference>), a variety of miseries (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">ver. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.16">16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">17</reference>), such as should be their reproach and ruin, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13-Ezek.5.15">ver. 13-15</reference>.
entries.242801f0517fed957b2711ca1f55e6a288fb7409: <div eID="gen18466" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18465" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Representation of Jerusalem's Ruin. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18467" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's razor, and cause <hi type="italic">it</hi> to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the <hi type="italic">hair.</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, <hi type="italic">and</hi> smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then take of them again, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; <hi type="italic">for</hi> thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel. <div eID="gen18467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18468" type="x-p"/> We have here the sign by which the utter destruction of Jerusalem is set forth; and here, as before, the prophet is himself the sign, that the people might see how much he affected himself with, and interested himself in, the case of Jerusalem, and how it lay to his heart, even when he foretold the desolations of it. He was so much concerned about it as to take what was done to it as done to himself, so far was he from desiring the woeful day. <div eID="gen18468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18469" type="x-p"/> I. He must <hi type="italic">shave off the hair of his head and beard</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.1">v. 1</reference>), which signified God's utter rejecting and abandoning that people, as a useless worthless generation, such as could well be spared, nay, such as it would be his honour to part with; his judgments, and all the instruments he made use of in cutting them off, were this <hi type="italic">sharp knife</hi> and this <hi type="italic">razor,</hi> that were proper to be made use of, and would do execution. Jerusalem had been the head, but, having degenerated, had become as the <hi type="italic">hair,</hi> which, when it grows thick and long, is but a burden which a man wishes to get clear of, as God of the sinners in Zion. <hi type="italic">Ah! I will ease me of my adversaries,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa. i. 24</reference>. Ezekiel must not cut off that hair only which was superfluous, but <hi type="italic">cut it all off,</hi> denoting the full end that God would make of Jerusalem. The hair that would not be trimmed and kept neat and clean by the admonitions of the prophets must be all shaved off by utter destruction. Those will be ruined that will not be reformed. <div eID="gen18469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18470" type="x-p"/> II. He must <hi type="italic">weigh the hair</hi> and <hi type="italic">divide it into three parts.</hi> This intimates the very exact directing of God's judgments according to equity (by him men and their actions are <hi type="italic">weighed</hi> in the unerring balance of truth and righteousness) and the proportion which divine justice observes in punishing some by one judgment and others by another; one way or other, they shall all be met with. Some make the shaving of the hair to denote the loss of their liberty and of their honour: it was looked upon as a mark of ignominy, as in the disgrace Hanun put on David's ambassadors. It denotes also the loss of their joy, for they shaved their heads upon occasion of great mourning; I may add the loss of their Nazariteship, for the shaving of the head was a period to that vow (<reference osisRef="Num.6.18">Num. vi. 18</reference>), and Jerusalem was now no longer looked upon as a <hi type="italic">holy city.</hi> <div eID="gen18470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18471" type="x-p"/> III. He must dispose of the hair so that it might all be destroyed or dispersed, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. One <hi type="italic">third part</hi> must <hi type="italic">be burnt in the midst of the city,</hi> denoting the multitudes that should perish by famine and pestilence, and perhaps many in the conflagration of the city, <hi type="italic">when the days of the siege were fulfilled.</hi> Or the laying of that glorious city in ashes might well be looked upon as a third part of the destruction threatened. 2. Another third part was to be <hi type="italic">cut in pieces with a knife,</hi> representing the many who, during the siege, were slain by the sword, in their sallies out upon the besiegers, and especially when the city was taken by storm, the Chaldeans being then most furious and the Jews most feeble. 3. Another third part was to be <hi type="italic">scattered in the wind,</hi> denoting the carrying away of some into the land of the conqueror and the flight of others into the neighbouring countries for shelter; so that they were hurried, some one way and some another, like loose hairs in the wind. But, lest they should think that this dispersion would be their escape, God adds, <hi type="italic">I will draw out a sword after them,</hi> so that wherever they go evil shall pursue them. Note, God has variety of judgments wherewith to accomplish the destruction of a sinful people and to make an end when he begins. <div eID="gen18471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18472" type="x-p"/> IV. He must preserve a small quantity of the third sort that were to be <hi type="italic">scattered in the wind,</hi> and <hi type="italic">bind them in his skirts,</hi> as one would bind that which he is very mindful and careful of, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.3">v. 3</reference>. This signified perhaps that little handful of people which were left under the government of Gedaliah, who, it was hoped, would keep possession of the land when the body of the people was carried into captivity. Thus God would have done well for them if they would have done well for themselves. But these few that were reserved must be taken and <hi type="italic">cast into the fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.4">v. 4</reference>. When Gedaliah and his friends were slain the people that put themselves under his protection were scattered, some gone into Egypt, others carried off by the Chaldeans, and in short the land totally cleared of them; then this was fulfilled, for out of those combustions <hi type="italic">a fire came forth into all the house of Israel,</hi> who, as fuel upon the fire, kindled and consumed one another. Note, It is ill with a people when those are taken away in wrath that seemed to be marked for monuments of mercy; for then there is no remnant or escaping, none shut up or left.
entries.ca7a6fa58c9300363e0682ebcdedfb68dc6b9f55: <div eID="gen18472" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Guilt of Jerusalem; The Punishment of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18473" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; This <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries <hi type="italic">that are</hi> round about her. <hi type="super">6</hi> And she hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries that <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about her: for they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because ye multiplied more than the nations that <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about you, <hi type="italic">and</hi> have not walked in my statutes, neither have kept my judgments, neither have done according to the judgments of the nations that <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about you; <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I, even I, <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, and will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations. <hi type="super">9</hi> And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds. <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherefore, <hi type="italic">as</hi> I live, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish <hi type="italic">thee;</hi> neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity. <hi type="super">12</hi> A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee: and a third part shall fall by the sword round about thee; and I will scatter a third part into all the winds, and I will draw out a sword after them. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it</hi> in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them. <hi type="super">14</hi> Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by. <hi type="super">15</hi> So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about thee, when I shall execute judgments in thee in anger and in fury and in furious rebukes. I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> When I shall send upon them the evil arrows of famine, which shall be for <hi type="italic">their</hi> destruction, <hi type="italic">and</hi> which I will send to destroy you: and I will increase the famine upon you, and will break your staff of bread: <hi type="super">17</hi> So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee; and pestilence and blood shall pass through thee; and I will bring the sword upon thee. I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen18473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18474" type="x-p"/> We have here the explanation of the foregoing similitude: <hi type="italic">This is Jerusalem.</hi> Thus it is usual in scripture language to give the name of the thing signified to the sign; as when Christ said, <hi type="italic">This is my body.</hi> The prophet's head, which was to be shaved, signified Jerusalem, which by the judgments of God was now to be stripped of all its ornaments, to be emptied of all its inhabitants, and to be set <hi type="italic">naked and bare,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">shaved with a razor that is hired,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">Isa. vii. 20</reference>. The head of one that was a priest, a prophet, a holy person, was fittest to represent Jerusalem the holy city. Now the contents of these verses are much the same with what we have often met with, and still shall, in the writings of the prophets. Here we have, <div eID="gen18474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18475" type="x-p"/> I. The privileges Jerusalem was honoured with (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her,</hi> and those famous nations and very considerable. Jerusalem was not situated in a remote obscure corner of the world, far from neighbours, but in the midst of kingdoms that were populous, polite, and civilized, famed for learning, arts, and sciences, and which then made the greatest figure in the world. But there seems to be more in it than this. 1. Jerusalem was dignified and preferred above the neighbouring nations and their cities. it was <hi type="italic">set in the midst</hi> of them as excelling them all. This <hi type="italic">holy mountain was exalted above all the hills,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa. ii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Why leap you, you high hills? This is the hill which God desires to dwell in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.16">Ps. lxviii. 16</reference>. Jerusalem was a city upon a hill, conspicuous and illustrious, and which all the neighbouring nations had an eye upon, some for good-will, some for ill-will. 2. Jerusalem was designed to have a good influence upon <hi type="italic">the nations and countries round about,</hi> was set in the midst of them as a candle upon a candlestick, to spread the light of divine revelation, which she was blessed with, to all the dark corners of the neighbouring nations, that from them it might diffuse itself further, even to the ends of the earth. Jerusalem was set <hi type="italic">in the midst</hi> of the nations, to be as the heart in the body, to invigorate this dead world with a divine life as well as to enlighten this dark world with a divine light, to be an example of every thing that was good. The nations that observed what excellent <hi type="italic">statutes and judgments</hi> they had concluded them to be <hi type="italic">a wise and understanding people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deut. iv. 6</reference>), fit to be consulted as an oracle, as they were in Solomon's time, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.34">1 Kings iv. 34</reference>. And, had they preserved this reputation and made a right use of it, what a blessing would Jerusalem have been to all the nations about! But, failing to be so, the accomplishment of this intention was reserved for its latter days, <hi type="italic">when out of Zion went forth the</hi> gospel <hi type="italic">law and the word of the Lord</hi> Jesus <hi type="italic">from Jerusalem,</hi> and there <hi type="italic">repentance and remission</hi> began to be preached, and thence the preachers of them <hi type="italic">went forth into all nations.</hi> And, when that was done, Jerusalem was levelled with the ground. Note, When places and persons are made great, it is with design that they may do good and that those about them may be the better for them, that their <hi type="italic">light may shine before men.</hi> <div eID="gen18475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18476" type="x-p"/> II. The provocations Jerusalem was guilty of. A very high charge is here drawn up against that city, and proved beyond contradiction sufficient to justify God in seizing its privileges and putting it under military execution. 1. She has <hi type="italic">not walked in God's statutes,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">kept his judgments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">v. 7</reference>); nay, the inhabitants of Jerusalem had <hi type="italic">refused his judgments and his statutes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.6">v. 6</reference>); they did not do their duty, nay, they <hi type="italic">would not,</hi> they said that they would not. Those <hi type="italic">statutes and judgments</hi> which their neighbours admired they despised, which they should have set before their face they cast behind their back. Note, A contempt of the word and law of God opens a door to all manner of iniquity. God's statutes are the terms on which he deals with men; those that refuse his terms cannot expect his favours. 2. She had <hi type="italic">changed God's judgments into wickedness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.6">v. 6</reference>), a very high expression of profaneness, that the people had not only broken God's laws, but had so perverted and abused them that they had made them the excuse and colour of their wickedness. They introduced the abominable customs and usages of the heathen, instead of God's institutions; this was changing <hi type="italic">the truth of God into a lie</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.25">Rom. i. 25</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">glory of God into shame,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Ps. iv. 2</reference>. Note, Those that have been well educated, if they live ill, put the highest affront imaginable upon God, as if he were the patron of sin and <hi type="italic">his judgments</hi> were <hi type="italic">turned into wickedness.</hi> 3. She had been worse than the neighbouring nations, to whom she should have set a good example: <hi type="italic">She has changed my judgments,</hi> by idolatries and false worship, <hi type="italic">more than the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.6">v. 6</reference>), and she has <hi type="italic">multiplied</hi> (that is, multiplied idols and altars, gods and temples, multiplied those things the unity of which was their praise) <hi type="italic">more than the nations that were round about.</hi> Israel's God is one, and his name one, his altar one; but they, not content with this one God, multiplied their gods to such a degree that <hi type="italic">according to the number of their cities so were their gods,</hi> and their altars were <hi type="italic">as heaps in the furrows of the field;</hi> so that they exceeded all their neighbours in having <hi type="italic">gods many and lords many.</hi> They corrupted revealed religion more than the Gentiles had corrupted natural religion. Note, If those who have made a profession of religion, and have had a pious education, apostatize from it, they are commonly more profane and vicious than those who never made any profession; they have <hi type="italic">seven other spirits more wicked.</hi> 4. She had <hi type="italic">not done according to the judgments of the nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Israel had not acted towards their God, as the nations had acted towards their gods, though they were false gods; they had not been so observant of him nor so constant to him. Has a nation <hi type="italic">changed its gods,</hi> or slighted them, so as they have? <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jer. ii. 11</reference>. Or it may refer to their morals; instead of reforming their neighbors, they came short of them; and many who were of the <hi type="italic">uncircumcision kept the righteousness of the law</hi> better than those who were <hi type="italic">of the circumcision,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.26-Rom.2.27">Rom. ii. 26, 27</reference>. Those who had the light of scripture did not <hi type="italic">according to the judgments</hi> of many who had only the light of nature. Note, There are those who are called <hi type="italic">Christians</hi> who will in the great day be condemned by the better tempers and better lives of sober heathens. 5. The particular crime charged upon Jerusalem is profaning the holy things, which she had been both entrusted and honoured with (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things,</hi> with thy idols and idolatries. The images of their pretended deities, and the groves erected in honour of them, were brought into the temple; and the ceremonies used by idolaters were brought into the worship of God. Thus every thing that is sacred was polluted. Note, Idols are detestable things any where, but more especially so in the sanctuary. <div eID="gen18476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18477" type="x-p"/> III. The punishments that Jerusalem should fall under for these provocations: <hi type="italic">Shall not God visit for these things?</hi> No doubt he shall. The matter of the sentence here passed upon Jerusalem is very dreadful, and the manner of expression makes it yet more so; the judgments are various, and the threatenings of them varied, reiterated, inculcated, that one may well say, <hi type="italic">Who is able to stand in God's sight when once he is angry?</hi> <div eID="gen18477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18478" type="x-p"/> 1. God will take this work of punishing Jerusalem into his own hands; and <hi type="italic">who knows the power of his anger</hi> and what <hi type="italic">a fearful thing it is to fall into his hands?</hi> Observe what a strong emphasis is laid upon it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">I, even I, am against thee.</hi> God had been for Jerusalem, to defend and save it; but miserable is its case when he has turned to be its enemy and fights against it. If God be against us, the whole creation is at war with us, and nothing can be for us so as to stand us in any stead: "You think it is only the Chaldean army that is against you, but they are God's hand, or rather the staff in his hand; it is <hi type="italic">I, even I,</hi> that <hi type="italic">am against thee,</hi> not only to speak against thee by prophets, but to act against thee by providence. <hi type="italic">I will execute judgments in thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">in the midst of thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.8">v. 8</reference>), not only in the suburbs, but in the heart of the city, not only in the borders, but in the bowels of the country." Note, Those who will not observe the judgments of God's mouth shall not escape the judgments of his hand; and God's judgments, when they come with commission, will penetrate into the midst of a people, will enter into the soul, <hi type="italic">into the bowels like water</hi> and <hi type="italic">like oil into the bones. I will execute judgments.</hi> Note, God himself undertakes to execute his own judgments, according to the true and full intent of them; whatever are the instruments, he is the principal agent. <div eID="gen18478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18479" type="x-p"/> 2. These punishments shall come from his displeasure. As to the body of the people, it shall not be a correction in love, but he will <hi type="italic">execute judgments in anger, and in fury, and in furious rebukes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.15">v. 15</reference>), strange expressions to come from a God who has said, <hi type="italic">Fury is not in me,</hi> and who has declared himself <hi type="italic">gracious, and merciful,</hi> and <hi type="italic">slow to anger.</hi> But they are designed to show the malignity of sin, and the offence it gives to the just and holy God. That must needs be a very evil thing which provokes him to such resentments, and against his own people too, that had been so high in his favour, and expressed with so much satisfaction (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My anger,</hi> which has long been withheld, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> now <hi type="italic">be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them;</hi> it shall not only light upon them, but lie upon them, and fill them as vessels of wrath fitted by their own wickedness to destruction; <hi type="italic">and,</hi> justice being hereby glorified, <hi type="italic">I will be comforted,</hi> I will be entirely satisfied in what I have done." As, when God is dishonoured by the sins of men, he is said to be <hi type="italic">grieved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Ps. xcv. 10</reference>), so when he is honoured by their destruction he is said to <hi type="italic">be comforted.</hi> The struggle between mercy and judgment is over, and in this case judgment triumphs, triumphs indeed; for mercy that has been so long abused is now silent and gives up the cause, has not a word more to say on the behalf of such an ungrateful incorrigible people: <hi type="italic">My eye shall not spare, neither will I have any pity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">v. 11</reference>. Divine compassion defers the punishment, or mitigates it, or supports under it, or shortens it; but here is <hi type="italic">judgment without mercy,</hi> wrath without any mixture or allay of pity. These expressions are thus sharpened and heightened perhaps with design to look further, to the vengeance of eternal fire, which some of the destructions we read of in the Old Testament were typical of, and particularly that of Jerusalem; for surely it is nowhere on this side hell that this word has its full accomplishment, <hi type="italic">My eye shall not spare,</hi> but <hi type="italic">I will cause my fury to rest.</hi> Note, Those who live and die impenitent will perish for ever unpitied; there is a day coming when <hi type="italic">the Lord will not spare.</hi> <div eID="gen18479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18480" type="x-p"/> 3. Punishments shall be public and open: <hi type="italic">I will execute</hi> these <hi type="italic">judgments in the sight of the nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.8">v. 8</reference>); the judgments themselves shall be so remarkable that all the nations far and near shall take notice of them; they shall be all the talk of that part of the world, and the more for the conspicuousness of the place and people on which they are inflicted. Note, Public sins, as they call for public reproofs (<hi type="italic">those that sin rebuke before all</hi>), so, if those prevail not, they call for public judgments. <hi type="italic">He strikes them as wicked men in the open sight of others</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job xxxiv. 26</reference>), that he may maintain and vindicate the honour of his government, for (as Grotius descants upon it here) <hi type="italic">why should he suffer it to be said, See what wicked lives those lead who profess to be the worshippers of the only true God!</hi> And, as the publicity of the judgments will redound to the honour of God, so it will serve, (1.) To aggravate the punishment, and to make it lie the more heavily. Jerusalem, being made <hi type="italic">waste,</hi> becomes <hi type="italic">a reproach among the nations in the sight of all that pass by,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.14">v. 14</reference>. The more conspicuous and the more peculiar any have been in the day of their prosperity the greater disgrace attends their fall; and that was Jerusalem's case. The more Jerusalem had been <hi type="italic">a praise in the earth</hi> the more it is now <hi type="italic">a reproach and a taunt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.15">v. 15</reference>. This she was warned of as much as any thing when her glory commenced (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1 Kings ix. 8</reference>), and this was lamented as much as any thing when it was laid in the dust, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam. ii. 15</reference>. (2.) To teach the nations to fear before the God of Israel, when they see what a jealous God he is, and how severely he punishes sin even in those that are nearest to him: <hi type="italic">It shall be an instruction to the nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.15">v. 15</reference>. Jerusalem should have taught her neighbours the fear of God by her piety and virtue, but, she not doing that, God will teach it to them by her ruin; for they have reason to say, <hi type="italic">If this be done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?</hi> If <hi type="italic">judgment begin at the house of God,</hi> where will it end? If those be thus punished who only had some idolaters among them, what will become of us who are all idolaters? Note, The destruction of some is designed for the instruction of others. Malefactors are publicly punished <hi type="italic">in terrorem</hi>—<hi type="italic">that others may take warning.</hi> <div eID="gen18480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18481" type="x-p"/> 4. These punishments, in the kind of them, shall be very severe and grievous. (1.) They shall be such as have no precedent or parallel. Their sins being more provoking than those of others, the judgments executed upon them should be uncommon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">"I will do in thee that which I have not done</hi> in thee before, though thou hast long since deserved it; nay, that which I have not done in any other city." This punishment of Jerusalem is said to be <hi type="italic">greater than that of Sodom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">Lam. iv. 6</reference>), which was more grievous than all that went before it; nay, it is such as "<hi type="italic">I will not do any more the like,</hi> all the circumstances taken in, to any other city, till the like come to be done again to this city, in the final overthrow by the Romans." This is a rhetorical expression of the most grievous judgments, like that character of Hezekiah, that there was <hi type="italic">none like him, before or after him.</hi> (2.) They shall be such as will force them to break the strongest bonds of natural affection to one another, which will be a just punishment of them for their wilfully breaking the bonds of their duty to God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The fathers shall eat the sons, and the sons shall eat the fathers,</hi> through the extremity of the famine, or shall be compelled to do it by their barbarous conquerors. (3.) There shall be a complication of judgments, any one of them terrible enough, and desolating; but what then would they be when they came all together and in perfection? Some shall be taken away by the plague (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">v. 12</reference>); the <hi type="italic">pestilence shall pass through thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">v. 17</reference>), sweeping all before it, as the destroying angel; others <hi type="italic">shall be consumed with famine,</hi> shall gradually waste away as men in a consumption (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">v. 12</reference>); this is again insisted on (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will send upon them the evil arrows of famine;</hi> hunger shall make them pine, and shall pierce them to the heart, as if arrows, <hi type="italic">evil arrows,</hi> poisoned darts, were shot into them. God has many arrows, <hi type="italic">evil arrows,</hi> in his quiver; when some are discharged, he has still more in reserve. <hi type="italic">I will increase the famine upon you.</hi> A famine in a bereaved country may <hi type="italic">decrease</hi> as fruits spring forth; but a famine in a besieged city will <hi type="italic">increase</hi> of course; yet God speaks of it as his act: "<hi type="italic">I will increase it, and will break your staff of bread,</hi> will take away the necessary supports of life, will disappoint you of all that which you depend upon, so that there is no remedy, but you must fall to the ground." Life is frail, is weak, is burdened, so that, if it have not daily bread for its staff to lean upon, it cannot but sink, and is soon gone if that staff be broken. Others <hi type="italic">shall fall by the sword round about</hi> Jerusalem, when they sally out upon the besiegers; it is a <hi type="italic">sword</hi> which God <hi type="italic">will bring,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">v. 17</reference>. The sword of the Lord, that used to be drawn for Jerusalem's defence, is now drawn for its destruction. Others are devoured by <hi type="italic">evil beasts,</hi> which will make a prey of those that fly for shelter to the deserts and mountains. They shall meet their ruin where they expected refuge, for there is no escaping the judgments of God, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">v. 17</reference>. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> those who escape shall be <hi type="italic">scattered into</hi> all parts of the world, <hi type="italic">into all the winds</hi> (so it is expressed, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">12</reference>), intimating that they should not only be dispersed, but hurried, and tossed, and driven to and fro, as <hi type="italic">chaff before the wind.</hi> Nay, and Cain's curse (to be fugitives and vagabonds) is not the worst of it neither; their restless life shall be cut off by a bloody death: "<hi type="italic">I will draw out a sword after them,</hi> which shall follow them wherever they go." <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners;</hi> and the curse shall come upon them and overtake them. <div eID="gen18481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18482" type="x-p"/> 5. These punishments will prove their ruin by degrees. They shall be <hi type="italic">diminished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">v. 11</reference>); their strength and glory shall grow less and less. They shall be <hi type="italic">bereaved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">v. 17</reference>), emptied of all that which was their joy and confidence. God sends these judgments on purpose to destroy them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.16">v. 16</reference>. The arrows are not sent (as those which Jonathan shot) for their direction, but <hi type="italic">for their destruction;</hi> for God will <hi type="italic">accomplish his fury upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">v. 13</reference>); the day of God's patience is over, and the ruin is remediless. Though this prophecy was to have its accomplishment now quickly, in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, yet the executioners not being named here, but the criminal only (<hi type="italic">this is Jerusalem</hi>), we may well suppose that it looks further, to the final destruction of that great city by the Romans when God made a full end of the Jewish nation, and <hi type="italic">caused his fury to rest upon them.</hi> <div eID="gen18482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18483" type="x-p"/> 6. All this is ratified by the divine authority and veracity: <hi type="italic">I the Lord have spoken it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.15">v. 15</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.17">v. 17</reference>. The sentence is passed by him that is Judge of heaven and earth, whose <hi type="italic">judgment is according to truth,</hi> and the judgments of whose hand are according to the judgments of his mouth. He has spoken it who can do it, for with him nothing is impossible. He has spoken it who will do it, for <hi type="italic">he is not a man that he should lie.</hi> He has spoken it whom we are bound to hear and heed, whose <hi type="italic">ipse dixit—word</hi> commands the most serious attention and submissive assent: <hi type="italic">And they shall know that I the Lord have spoken it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">v. 13</reference>. There were those who thought it was only the prophet that spoke it in his delirium; but God will make them know, by the accomplishment of it, that he has spoken it in his zeal. Note, Sooner or later, God's word will prove itself.  <chapter eID="Ezek.5"/> <div eID="gen18483" type="x-p"/>

entries.f78d8bbbdb252110003a0e8aaf1d63af005aa8fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11019"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.5.1-Ezek.5.17">Eze 5:1-17</reference>. Vision of Cutting the Hairs, and the Calamities Foreshadowed Thereby.</title> <div sID="gen19848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11019"/><hi type="bold">1. knife ... razor--</hi>the sword of the foe (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">Is 7:20</reference>). This vision implies even severer judgments than the Egyptian afflictions foreshadowed in the former, for their guilt was greater than that of their forefathers.<div eID="gen19848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine head--</hi>as representative of the Jews. The whole hair being shaven off was significant of severe and humiliating (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sa 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">5</reference>) treatment. Especially in the case of a priest; for priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.5">Le 21:5</reference>) were forbidden "to make baldness on their head," their hair being the token of consecration; hereby it was intimated that the ceremonial must give place to the moral.<div eID="gen19849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">balances--</hi>implying the just discrimination with which Jehovah weighs out the portion of punishment "divided," that is, allotted to each: the "hairs" are the Jews: the divine scales do not allow even one hair to escape accurate weighing (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.10.30">Mt 10:30</reference>). <div eID="gen19850" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2443a8f6aaef2fcb5e9d87005e86c0ccc46b653: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11020"/><div sID="gen19851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11020"/>2. Three classes are described. The sword was to destroy one third of the people; famine and plague another third ("fire" in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference> being explained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">Eze 5:12</reference> to mean pestilence and famine); that which remained was to be scattered among the nations. A few only of the last portion were to escape, symbolized by the hairs bound in Ezekiel's skirts (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.3">Eze 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.6">Jr 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">52:16</reference>). Even of these some were to be thrown into the fiery ordeal again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.4">Eze 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.41.1">Jr 41:1</reference>, 2, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">Jr 44:14</reference>, &c.). The "skirts" being able to contain but few express that extreme limit to which God's goodness can reach. <div eID="gen19851" type="x-p"/>
entries.611c35c43e135b6e66c19fae1c077c7b354fe301: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11021"/><div sID="gen19852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11021"/>5-6. Explanation of the symbols:<div eID="gen19852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>not the mere city, but the people of Israel generally, of which it was the center and representative.<div eID="gen19853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst--</hi>Jerusalem is regarded in God's point of view as center of the whole earth, designed to radiate the true light over the nations in all directions. Compare Margin ("navel"), <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.12">Eze 38:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>. No center in the ancient heathen world could have been selected more fitted than Canaan to be a vantage ground, whence the people of God might have acted with success upon the heathenism of the world. It lay midway between the oldest and most civilized states, Egypt and Ethiopia on one side, and Babylon, Nineveh, and India on the other, and afterwards Persia, Greece, and Rome. The Phoenician mariners were close by, through whom they might have transmitted the true religion to the remotest lands; and all around the Ishmaelites, the great inland traders in South Asia and North Africa. Israel was thus placed, not for its own selfish good, but to be the spiritual benefactor of the whole world. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.67.1-Ps.67.7">Psa 67:1-7</reference> throughout. Failing in this, and falling into idolatry, its guilt was far worse than that of the heathen; not that Israel literally went beyond the heathen in abominable idolatries. But "corruptio optimi pessima"; the perversion of that which in itself is the best is worse than the perversion of that which is less perfect: is in fact the worst of all kinds of perversion. Therefore their punishment was the severest. So the position of the Christian professing Church now, if it be not a light to the heathen world, its condemnation will be sorer than theirs (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.13">Mt 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21-Matt.11.24">11:21-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.28">He 10:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">29</reference>). <div eID="gen19854" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f354bb54746aac848ace4d0aa8452b5404a8e75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11023"/><div sID="gen19856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11023"/><hi type="bold">7. multiplied--</hi>rather, "have been more abundantly outrageous"; literally, "to tumultuate"; to have an extravagant rage for idols.<div eID="gen19856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither have done according to the judgments of the nations--</hi>have not been as tenacious of the true religion as the nations have been of the false. The heathen "changed" not their gods, but the Jews changed Jehovah for idols (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.6">Eze 5:6</reference>, "changed My judgments into wickedness," that is, idolatry, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jr 2:11</reference>). The Chaldean version and the Masora support the negative. Others omit it (as it is omitted in <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:12</reference>), and translate, "but have done according to the judgments," &c. However, both <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:12</reference> and also this verse are true. They in one sense "did according to the heathen," namely, in all that was bad; in another, namely, in that which was good, zeal for religion, they did not. <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.9">Eze 5:9</reference> also proves the negative to be genuine; because in changing their religion, they have not done as the nations which have not changed theirs, "I (also) will do in thee that which I have not done." <div eID="gen19857" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d9e6930131eedf973d20fa3bc04e8f211f0c686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11024"/><div sID="gen19858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11024"/><hi type="bold">8. I, even I--</hi>awfully emphatic. I, even I, whom thou thinkest to be asleep, but who am ever reigning as the Omnipotent Avenger of sin, will vindicate My righteous government before the nations by judgments on thee. <div eID="gen19858" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f0b5e4abb8a84ddbf86c128b5d3c9777484002c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11025"/><div sID="gen19859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11025"/>9. See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">Eze 5:7</reference>.<div eID="gen19859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which I have not done--</hi>worse than any former judgments (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">La 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.12">Da 9:12</reference>). The prophecy includes the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, and the final one by Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>), as well as that by Nebuchadnezzar. Their doom of evil was not exhausted by the Chaldean conquest. There was to be a germinating evil in their destiny, because there would be, as the Lord foresaw, a germinating evil in their character. As God connected Himself peculiarly with Israel, so there was to be a peculiar manifestation of God's wrath against sin in their case [Fairbairn]. The higher the privileges the greater the punishment in the case of abuse of them. When God's greatest favor, the gospel, was given, and was abused by them, then "the wrath was to come on them to the uttermost" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1Th 2:16</reference>). <div eID="gen19860" type="x-p"/>
entries.77c19c72e6b753eb66ebc7be2bb6c78e9d52bfbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11026"/><div sID="gen19861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11026"/><hi type="bold">10. fathers ... eat ... sons--</hi>alluding to Moses' words (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Le 26:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">De 28:53</reference>), with the additional sad feature, that "the sons should eat their fathers" (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.28">2Ki 6:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jr 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">La 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen19861" type="x-p"/>
entries.e10e92ac0ae370b750bdfa65b522293439d6bd61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11027"/><div sID="gen19862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11027"/><hi type="bold">11. as I live--</hi>the most solemn of oaths, pledging the self-existence of God for the certainty of the event.<div eID="gen19862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defiled my sanctuary--</hi>the climax of Jewish guilt: their defiling Jehovah's temple by introducing idols.<div eID="gen19863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diminish--</hi>literally, "withdraw," namely, Mine "eye" (which presently follows), that is, My favors; <reference osisRef="Job.36.7">Job 36:7</reference> uses the Hebrew verb in the same way. As the Jews had withdrawn from God's sanctuary its sacredness by "defiling" it, so God withdraws His countenance from them. The significance of the expression lies in the allusion to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">De 4:2</reference>, "Ye shall not diminish aught from the word which I command you"; they had done so, therefore God diminishes them. The reading found in six manuscripts, "I will cut thee off," is not so good. <div eID="gen19864" type="x-p"/>
entries.24205fbd6c1285de2e3fa23ba16e81671676f10b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11028"/><div sID="gen19865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11028"/>12. Statement in plain terms of what was intended by the symbols (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jr 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">21:9</reference>).<div eID="gen19865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw out ... sword after them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">Le 26:33</reference>). Skeptics object; no such thing happened under Zedekiah, as is here foretold; namely, that a third part of the nation should die by pestilence, a third part by the sword, and a third be scattered unto all winds, and a sword sent after them. But the prophecy is not restricted to Zedekiah's time. It includes all that Israel suffered, or was still to suffer, for their sins, especially those committed at that period (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.21">Eze 17:21</reference>). It only received its primary fulfilment under Zedekiah: numbers then died by the pestilence and by the sword; and numbers were scattered in all quarters and not carried to Babylonia alone, as the objectors assert (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.4">Ezr 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.3.8">Es 3:8</reference>; Ob 14).<div eID="gen19866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pestilence ... and famine--</hi>signified by the symbol "fire" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.2">Eze 5:2</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.13.8">Is 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.10">La 5:10</reference>; plague and famine burning and withering the countenance, as fire does. <div eID="gen19867" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d0f03b800c4bbf4de8f1da7e26e06fa52dc9a4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11029"/><div sID="gen19868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11029"/><hi type="bold">13. cause my fury to rest upon them--</hi>as on its proper and permanent resting-place (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">Is 30:32</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen19868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19869" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will be comforted--</hi>expressed in condescension to man's conceptions; signifying His satisfaction in the vindication of His justice by His righteous judgments (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.63">De 28:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.26">Pr 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Is 1:24</reference>).<div eID="gen19869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall how--</hi>by bitter experience. <div eID="gen19870" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc6919bfa31909ae45a0ca22ac5e73d897704a2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11030"/><div sID="gen19871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11030"/><hi type="bold">14. reproach among the nations--</hi>They whose idolatries Israel had adopted, instead of comforting, would only exult in their calamities brought on by those idolatries (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.15.15">Lu 15:15</reference>). <div eID="gen19871" type="x-p"/>
entries.04f25189d5f95e993f9a2511ce515d7241a37f25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11031"/><div sID="gen19872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11031"/><hi type="bold">15. instruction--</hi>literally, "a corrective chastisement," that is, a striking example to warn all of the fatal consequences of sin. For "it shall be"; all ancient versions have "thou," which the connection favors. <div eID="gen19872" type="x-p"/>
entries.89bc2bedee065b0f238ce811419aee28a4f0b8e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11032"/><div sID="gen19873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11032"/><hi type="bold">16. arrows of famine--</hi>hail, rain, mice, locusts, mildew (see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.23">De 32:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen19873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">increase the famine--</hi>literally, "congregate" or "collect." When ye think your harvest safe because ye have escaped drought, mildew, &c., I will find other means [Calvin], which I will congregate as the forces of an invading army, to bring famine on you. <div eID="gen19874" type="x-p"/>
entries.218c009a41f4ad5152284f9fb95f7d991ffc911b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11033"/><div sID="gen19875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11033"/><hi type="bold">17. beasts--</hi>perhaps meaning destructive conquerors (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.4">Da 7:4</reference>). Rather, literal "beasts," which infest desolated regions such as Judea was to become (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.28">Eze 34:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.29">Ex 23:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.24">De 32:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.25">2Ki 17:25</reference>). The same threat is repeated in manifold forms to awaken the careless.<div eID="gen19875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword--</hi>civil war. <chapter eID="Ezek.5"/>

entries.26aefce6881d675aefb62591dbda462645b62c82: <div eID="gen31318" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31319" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31320" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31320" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31319" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31321" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the prophet shows, under the type of hair, the judgments which God was about to execute on the inhabitants of Jerusalem by famine, sword, and dispersion, <reference osisRef="Eze.5.14">Eze 5:14</reference>. The type or allegory is then dropped, and God is introduced declaring in plain terms the vengeance that was coming on the whole nation which had proved so unworthy of those mercies with which they had hitherto been distinguished, <reference osisRef="Eze.5.5-Eze.5.17">Eze 5:5-17</reference>. <div eID="gen31321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31322" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31323" type="x-p"/> Take thee a sharp knife - Among the Israelites, and indeed among most ancient nations, there were very few edge-tools. The sword was the chief; and this was used as a knife, a razor, etc., according to its different length and sharpness. It is likely that only one kind of instrument is here intended; a knife or short sword, to be employed as a razor. <div eID="gen31323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31324" type="x-p"/> Here is a new emblem produced, in order to mark out the coming evils. <div eID="gen31324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31325" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophet represents the Jewish nation. <div eID="gen31325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31326" type="x-p"/> 2. His hair, the people. <div eID="gen31326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31327" type="x-p"/> 3. The razor, the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen31327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31328" type="x-p"/> 4. The cutting the beard and hair, the calamities, sorrows, and disgrace coming upon the people. Cutting off the hair was a sign of mourning; see on <reference osisRef="Jer.45.5">Jer 45:5</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jer 48:37</reference> (note); and also a sign of great disgrace; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference>. <div eID="gen31328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31329" type="x-p"/> 5. He is ordered to divide the hair, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.2">2Sam 10:2</reference>, into three equal parts, to intimate the different degrees and kinds of punishment which should fall upon the people. <div eID="gen31329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31330" type="x-p"/> 6. The balances, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1">2Sam 10:1</reference>, were to represent the Divine justice, and the exactness with which God's judgments should be distributed among the offenders. <div eID="gen31330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31331" type="x-p"/> 7. This hair, divided into three parts, is to be disposed of thus: <div eID="gen31331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31332" type="x-p"/> 1. A third part is to be burnt in the midst of the city, to show that so many should perish by famine and pestilence during the siege. <div eID="gen31332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31333" type="x-p"/> 2. Another third part he was to cut in small portions about the city, (that figure which he had pourtrayed upon the brick), to signify those who should perish in different sorties, and in defending the walls. <div eID="gen31333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31334" type="x-p"/> 3. And the remaining third part he was to scatter in the wind, to point out those who should be driven into captivity. And, <div eID="gen31334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31335" type="x-p"/> 4. The sword following them was intended to show that their lives should be at the will of their captors, and that many of them should perish by the sword in their dispersions. <div eID="gen31335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31336" type="x-p"/> 5. The few hairs which he was to take in his skirts, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">2Sam 10:3</reference>, was intended to represent those few Jews that should be left in the land under Gedaliah, after the taking of the city. <div eID="gen31336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31337" type="x-p"/> 6. The throwing a part of these last into the fire, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference>, was intended to show the miseries that these suffered in Judea, in Egypt, and finally in their being also carried away into Babylon on the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar. See these transactions particularly pointed out in the notes on Jeremiah, chapters 40, 41, 42. Some think that this prophecy may refer to the persecution of the Jews by Antiochus Epiphanes.
entries.e7dce79e8696b076b3f9f73397f47e7fb356716d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31338" type="x-p"/> This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations - I have made this city the most eminent and the most illustrious in the world. Some think that these words refer to its geographical situation, as being equally in the center of the habitable world. But any point on a globe is its center, no matter where laid down; and it would not be difficult to show that even this literal sense is tolerably correct. But the point which is the center of the greatest portion of land that can be exhibited on one hemisphere is the capital of the British empire. See my Sermon on the universal spread of the Gospel.
entries.b3c4ff920debfa1142676b88ed636dc1a188c9d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31339" type="x-p"/> She hath changed my judgments - God shows the reason why he deals with Jerusalem in greater severity than with the surrounding nations; because she was more wicked than they. Bad and idolatrous as they were, they had a greater degree of morality among them than the Jews had. Having fallen from the true God, they became more abominable than others in proportion to the height, eminence, and glory from which they had fallen. This is the common case of backsliders; they frequently, in their fall, become tenfold more the children of wrath than they were before.
entries.5bff6b834c6e8c8c9ca84743b4646cb1de17cc34: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31340" type="x-p"/> I will do in thee that which I have not done - The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was one of the greatest calamities that ever fell on any nation or place before; and that by the Romans under Titus exceeded all that has taken place since. These two sackages of that city have no parallel in the history of mankind.
entries.698b97a6a0db7e8bbf36ea498bd726870e8c9803: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31341" type="x-p"/> The fathers shall eat the sons - Though we have not this fact so particularly stated in history, yet we cannot doubt of it, considering the extremities to which they were reduced during the siege. The same is referred to by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">Lam 4:10</reference>. Even the women, who were remarkable for kindness and humanity, boiled their own children, and ate them during the siege. <div eID="gen31341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31342" type="x-p"/> Will I scatter into all the winds - Disperse you, by captivity, among all the nations of the earth.
entries.68df612a06ae6df8fa21ef3bdf82e14df6a2ce22: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31343" type="x-p"/> A third part of thee - See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.5.1-Eze.5.4">Eze 5:1-4</reference> (note).
entries.6e8ce9d36f904b454cd35d8c9c0718b29bb08655: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31344" type="x-p"/> I will cause my fury to rest - My displeasure, and the evidences of it, shall not be transient; they shall be permanent upon you, and among you. And is not this dreadfully true to the present day?
entries.ae36ec000436c7c9ad21757f3b51911f27f05957: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31345" type="x-p"/> The evil arrows of famine - Famine and pestilence are represented as poisoned arrows, inflicting death wherever they wound. The ancients represented them in the same way.
entries.95512f7bcfe7af68d131df96c8347343f7f420b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31346" type="x-p"/> So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee - Wild beasts always multiply in depopulated countries. In England, wolves abounded when the country was thinly peopled, it is now full of inhabitants, and there is not one wolf in the land. Nebuchadnezzar and his Chaldeans may be called here evil beasts. He is often compared to a lion, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jer 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>; on account of the ravages made by him and his Chaldean armies.  <chapter eID="Ezek.5"/> <div eID="gen31346" type="x-p"/>

entries.4ef3a5513416d996cbf82a33b44988e17e9e244d: Chap. V. 1-4. — The Sign which is to poetray Israel's impending Destiny. — <hi type="italic">Ver. 1. And thou, son of man, take to thyself a sharp sword, as a razor shalt thou take it to thyself, and go with it over thy head, and over thy chin, and take to thee scales, and divide it (the hair). Ver. 2, A third part burn with fire in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are accomplished: and take the (other) third, smite with the sword round about it: and the (re-maining) third scatter to the winds; and the sword will I draw out after them. Ver. 3. Yet take a few of them by number, and bind them in the skirt of thy garment. Ver. 4. And of these again take a few, and cast them into the fire, and burn them with fire; from, thence a fire shall go forth over the whole house of Israel.</hi> — The description of this sign is easily understood. תַּ֤עַר הַגַּלָּבִים֙, “razor of the barbers,” is the predicate, which is to be understood to the suffix in תִּקָּחֶ֣נָּה; and the clause states the purpose for which Ezekiel is to use the sharp sword — viz. as a razor, in order to cut off therewith the hair of his head and beard. The hair, when cut off, he is to divide into three parts with a pair of scales (the suffix in חִלַּקְתָּֽם refers <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> to the hair). The one third he is to burn in the city, i.e. not in the actual Jerusalem, but in the city, sketched on the brick, which he is symbolically besieging (<reference osisRef="Ezek.4.3">Eze 4:3</reference>). To the city also is to be referred the suffix in סְבִ֣יבוֹתֶ֔יהָ, ver. 2, as is placed beyond doubt by ver. 12. In the last clause of ver. 2, which is taken from <reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">Lev 26:33</reference>, the description of the sign passes over into its exposition, for אַחֲרֵיהֶֽם does not refer to the hair, but to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The significance also of this symbolical act is easily recognised, and is, moreover, stated in ver. 12. Ezekiel, in this act, represents the besieged Jerusalem. What he does to his hair, that will God do to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. As the hair of the prophet falls under the sword, used as a razor, so will the inhabitants of Jerusalem fall, when the city is captured, into destruction, and that verily an ignominious destruction. This idea is contained in the picture of the hair-cutting, which was a dishonour done to what forms the ornament of a man. See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference> sqq. A third of the same is to perish in the city. As the fire destroys the hair, so will pestilence and hunger consume the inhabitants of the beleaguered city (ver. 12). The second third will, on the capture of the city, fall by the sword in the environs (ver. 12) ; the last third will God scatter to the winds, and — as Moses has already threatened the people — will draw forth the sword after them, still to persecute and smite them (ver. 12). This sign is continued (vers. 3 and 4) in a second symbolical act, which shadows forth what is further to happen to the people when dispersed among the heathen. Of the third scattered to the winds, Ezekiel is to bind a small portion in the skirt of his garment. מִשָּׁ֖ם, “from thence,” refers not to הִשְׁלַישֽית, but, <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi>, to תּֽזֲרֶה לָרוהַ : “from the place where the third that is scattered to the winds is found” — i.e., as regards the subject-matter, of those who are to be found among the dispersion. The binding up into the בִּנָפֶֽים, “the corners or ends of the garment” (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.34">Jer 2:34</reference>), denotes the preservation of the few, who are gathered together out of the whole of those who are dispersed among the heathen ; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1Sam 25;29</reference>; Eze 16:8. But even of these few He shall still cast some into the fire, and consume them. Consequently those who are gathered together out of exile are not all to be preserved, but are still to be sifted by fire, in which process a part is consumed. This image does not refer to those who remain behind in the land, when the nation is led away captive to Babylon (Theodoret, Grotius, and others), but, as Ephrem the Syrian and Jerome saw, to those who were saved from Babylon, and to their further destiny, as is already clear from the מִשָּׁ֖ם, rightly understood. The meaning of the last clause of ver. 4 is disputed; in it, as in the final clause of ver. 2, the symbolical representation passes over into the announcement of the thing itself. טֽטֶנּוּ, which Ewald would arbitrarily alter into טֽטֶנּי, cannot, with Hävenick, be referred to אֶל־תּ֣וֹךְ הָאֵ֔שׁ, because this yields a very forced sense, but relates to the whole act described in vers. 3 and 4 : that a portion thereof is rescued and preserved, and yet of this portion many are consumed by fire, — from that a fire shall go forth over the whole house of Israel. This fire is explained by almost all expositors, from Theodoret and Jerome onwards, of the penal judgments which were inflicted after the exile upon the Jews, which reached their culminating point in the siege and destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, and which still continue in their dispersion throughout the whole world. But this view, as Kliefoth has already remarked, is not only in decided antagonism to the intention of the text, but it is, moreover, altogether impossible to see how a judgment of extermination for all Israel can be deduced from the fact that a small number of the Israelites, who are scattered to the winds, is saved, and that of those who are saved a part is still consumed with fire. From thence there can only come forth a fire of purification for the whole of Israel, through which the remnant, as Isaiah had already predicted (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.12">Eze 6:12</reference> sqq.), is converted into a holy seed. In the last clause, consuming by fire is not referred to. The fire, however, has not merely a destructive, but also a cleansing, purifying, and quickening power. To kindle such a fire on earth did Christ come (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.49">Luk 12:49</reference>), and from Him the same goes out over the whole house of Israel. This view, for which Kliefoth has already rightly decided, receives a confirmation through <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.8-Ezek.6.10">Eze 6:8-10</reference>, where is announced the conversion of the remnant of those Israelites who had been dispersed among the nations. So far the symbolical acts. Before, however, we pass on to the explanation of the following oracle, we must still briefly touch the question, whether these acts were undertaken and performed by the prophet in the world of external reality, or whether they were occurrences only internally real, which Ezekiel experienced in spirit — i.e. in an ecstatic condition — and afterwards communicated to the people. Amongst modem expositors, Kliefoth has defended the former view, and has adduced the following considerations in support : A significant act, and yet also a silent, leisurely one, must be performed, that it may show something to those who behold it. Nor is the case such, as Hitzig supposes, that it would have been impossible to carry out what had been required of the prophet in <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.1">Eze 4:1</reference>-17. It had, indeed, its difficulty; but God sometimes requires from His servants what is difficult, although He also helps them to the performance of it. So here He will make it easy for the prophet to recline, by binding him (iv. 8). “In the sign, this certainly was kept in view, that it should be performed; and it, moreover, was performed, although the test, in a manner quite intelligible with reference to an act commanded by God, does not expressly state it.” For these latter assertions, however, there is anything but convincing proof. The matter is not so simple as Kliefoth supposes, although we are at one with him in this, that neither the difficulty of carrying out what was commanded in the world of external reality, nor the non-mention of the actual performance, furnishes sufficient grounds for the supposition of merely internal, spiritual occurrences. We also are of opinion that very many of the symbolical acts of the prophets were undertaken and performed in the external world, and that this supposition, as that which corresponds most fully with the literal meaning of the words, is on each occasion the most obvious, and is to be firmly adhered to, unless there can be good grounds for the opposite view. In the case now before us, we have first to take into consideration that the oracle which enjoins these symbolical acts on Ezekiel stands in close connection, both as to time and place, with the inauguration of Ezekiel to the prophetic office. The hand of the Lord comes upon him at the same place, where the concluding word at his call was addressed to him (theשָׁ֖ם, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.22">Eze 3:22</reference>, points back to שָׁ֑ם in <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">Eze 3:15</reference>) ; and the circumstance that Ezekiel found himself still on the same spot to which he had been transported by the Spirit of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.14">Eze 3:14</reference>), shows that the new revelation, which he here still received, followed very soon, if not immediately, after his consecration to the office of prophet. Then, upon the occasion of this divine revelation, he is again, as at his consecration, transported into an ecstatic condition, as is clear not only from the formula, “the hand of the Lord came upon me,” which in our book always has this signification, but also most undoubtedly from this, that he again sees the glory of Jehovah in the same manner as he had seen it in Eze 1. — viz. when in an ecstatic condition. But if this were an ecstatic vision, it is obvious that the acts also which the divine appearance imposed upon him must be regarded as ecstatic occurrences ; since the assertion that every significant act must be performed, in order that something may be shown to those who witness it, is fundamentally insufficient for the proof that this act must fall within the domain of the earthly world of sense, because the occurrences related in Eze 8-11. are viewed even by Kliefoth himself as purely internal events. As decisive, however, for the purely internal character of the symbolical acts under consideration (Eze 4 and 5), is the circumstance that the supposition of Ezekiel having, in his own house, actually lain 390 days upon his left, and then, again, 40 days upon his right side without turning, stands in irreconcilable contradiction with the fact that he, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference> sqq., was carried away in ecstasy to Jerusalem, there to behold in the temple the monstrosities of Israel's idolatry and the destruction of Jerusalem. For the proof of this, see the introduction to Eze 8.
entries.66d905b0ea6b5a633a3c11615ef10686cadbc373: <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5-Ezek.5.9">Eze 5:5-9</reference> <div eID="gen14820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14821" type="x-p"/> The Divine Word which Explains the Symbolical Signs, in which the judgment that is announced is laid down as to its cause (5-9) and as to its nature (10-17). - Eze 5:5. <hi type="italic">Thus says the Lord Jehovah: This Jerusalem have I placed in the midst of the nations, and raised about her the countries.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.6">Eze 5:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. But in wickedness she resisted my laws more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries which are round about her; for they rejected my laws, and did not walk in my statutes.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">Eze 5:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. Therefore thus says the Lord Jehovah: Because ye have raged more than the nations round about you, and have not walked in my statutes, and have not obeyed my laws, and have not done even according to the laws of the nations which are round about you;</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.8">Eze 5:8</reference> <hi type="italic">. Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah: Lo, I, even I, shall be against thee, and will perform judgments in thy midst before the eyes of the nations.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.9">Eze 5:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I will do unto thee what I have never done, nor will again do in like manner, on account of all thine abominations.</hi> 'זאת ירוּשׁ not “this is Jerusalem,” i.e., this is the <hi type="italic">destiny</hi> of Jerusalem (Hävernick), but “this Jerusalem” (Hitzig); זאת is placed before the noun in the sense of <hi type="italic">iste</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.1">Exo 32:1</reference>; cf. Ewald, §293 <hi type="italic">b</hi>. To place the culpability of Jerusalem in its proper prominence, the censure of her sinful conduct opens with the mention of the exalted position which God had assigned her upon earth. Jerusalem is described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5">Eze 5:5</reference> as forming the central point of the earth: this is done, however, neither in an external, geographical (Hitzig), nor in a purely typical sense, as the city that is blessed more than any other (Calvin, Hävernick), but in a historical sense, in so far as “God’s people and city actually stand in the central point of the God-directed world-development and its movements” (Kliefoth); or, in relation to the history of salvation, as the city in which God hath set up His throne of grace, from which shall go forth the law and the statutes for all nations, in order that the salvation of the whole world may be accomplished (Isa 2:2.; Mic 4:1.). But instead of keeping the laws and statutes of the Lord, Jerusalem has, on the contrary, turned to do wickedness more than the heathen nations in all the lands round about (המרה, <hi type="italic">cum accusat. object</hi>., “to act rebelliously towards”). Here we may not quote <reference osisRef="Rom.2.12">Rom 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.2.14">Rom 2:14</reference> against this, as if the heathen, who did not know the law of God, did not also transgress the same, but sinned ἀνόμως; for the sinning ἀνόμως, of which the apostle speaks, is really a transgression of the law written on the heart of the heathen. With לכן, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">Eze 5:7</reference>, the penal threatening is introduced; but before the punishment is laid down, the correspondence between guilt and punishment is brought forward more prominently by repeatedly placing in juxtaposition the godless conduct of the rebellious city. המנכם is infinitive, from המן, a secondary form המון, in the sense of המה, “to rage,” i.e., to rebel against God; cf. Psa 2:1. The last clause of <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.7">Eze 5:7</reference> contains a climax: “And ye have not even acted according to the laws of the heathen.” This is not in any real contradiction to <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:12</reference> (where it is made a subject of reproach to the Israelites that they have acted according to the laws of the heathen), so that we would be obliged, with Ewald and Hitzig, to expunge the לא in the verse before us, because wanting in the Peshito and several Hebrew manuscripts. Even in these latter, it has only been omitted to avoid the supposed contradiction with Eze 11:12. The solution of the apparent contradiction lies in the double meaning of the משׁפּטי הּגוים. The heathen had laws which were opposed to those of God, but also such as were rooted in the law of God written upon their hearts. Obedience to the latter was good and praiseworthy; to the former, wicked and objectionable. Israel, which hated the law of God, followed the wicked and sinful laws of the heathen, and neglected to observe their <hi type="italic">good</hi> laws. The passage before us is to be judged by <reference osisRef="Jer.2.10-Jer.2.11">Jer 2:10-11</reference>, to which Raschi had already made reference.<note placement="foot">Coccejus had already well remarked on <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.12">Eze 11:12</reference> : <hi type="italic">”Haec probe concordant. Imitabantur Judaei gentiles vel fovendo opiniones gentiles, vel etiam assumendo ritus et sacra gentilium. Sed non faciebant ut gentes, quae integre diis suis serviebant. Nam Israelitae nomine Dei abutebantur et ipsius populus videri volebant.”</hi></note> <div eID="gen14821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14822" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.8">Eze 5:8</reference> the announcement of the punishment, interrupted by the repeated mention of the cause, is again resumed with the words 'לכן כּה וגו. Since Jerusalem has acted worse than the heathen, God will execute His judgments upon her before the eyes of the heathen. עשׂה שׁפטים or עשׂה (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Eze 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.15">Eze 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.9">Eze 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.41">Eze 16:41</reference>, etc.), “to accomplish or execute judgments,” is used in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exo 12:12</reference> and Num 33:4 of the judgments which God suspended over Egypt. The punishment to be suspended shall be so great and heavy, that the like has never happened before, nor will ever happen again. These words do not require us either to refer the threatening, with Coccejus, to the last destruction of Jerusalem, which was marked by greater severity than the earlier one, or to suppose, with Hävernick, that the prophet’s look is directed to both the periods of Israel’s punishment - the times of the Babylonian and Roman calamity together. Both suppositions are irreconcilable with the words, as these can only be referred to the first impending penal judgment of the destruction of Jerusalem. This was, so far, more severe than any previous or subsequent one, inasmuch as by it the existence of the people of God was for a time suspended, while that Jerusalem and Israel, which were destroyed and annihilated by the Romans, were no longer the people of God, inasmuch as the latter consisted at that time of the Christian community, which was not affected by that catastrophe (Kliefoth).
entries.22ef8c4c5fc9c4ef3523aa4e817195049c049e69: <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10-Ezek.5.17">Eze 5:10-17</reference> <div eID="gen14822" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Further Execution of this Threat</title> <div sID="gen14823" type="x-p"/> Eze 5:10. <hi type="italic">Therefore shall fathers devour their children in thy midst, and children shall devour their fathers: and I will exercise judgments upon thee, and disperse all thy remnant to the winds.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.11">Eze 5:11</reference> <hi type="italic">.
